nodes.languageNotes: Uses Server-Sent Events (SSE) on the `/session/:userId/qr` endpoint to stream QR code and connection state events to the frontend in real time.

nodes.name: session-manager.ts
nodes.summary: Core WhatsApp session lifecycle manager using `@whiskeysockets/baileys`, handling per-user session creation, QR/auth-state streaming, automatic reconnection on non-intentional disconnects, message sending, and bulk session restoration on startup.
nodes.languageNotes: Maintains two in-memory maps (`sessions`, `persistentListeners`) and uses an `intentionallyDisconnected` set to distinguish user-initiated logouts from unexpected disconnects, triggering exponential-style retry via `setTimeout`.

nodes.name: tsconfig.json
nodes.summary: TypeScript compiler configuration for the WhatsApp microservice, targeting ESNext with Node16 module resolution and strict mode enabled, compiling `src/` to a `dist/` output directory.

nodes.name: initSession
nodes.summary: Initialises a Baileys WhatsApp socket for a given user, attaches QR/connection-state event listeners that broadcast to registered SSE subscribers, and implements automatic reconnect with cleanup on unexpected disconnects.

nodes.name: subscribeToEvents
nodes.summary: Registers a persistent event listener for a user session, replaying current connection state immediately and returning an unsubscribe callback that cleans up both persistent and live-socket listener registrations.

nodes.name: disconnectSession
nodes.summary: Intentionally logs out and tears down a user's WhatsApp session, removing all in-memory state and deleting the persisted auth files from disk to prevent automatic reconnection.

nodes.name: restoreAllSessions
nodes.summary: Scans the sessions directory on service startup and reinitialises Baileys sessions for each persisted user directory in parallel, enabling warm restarts without requiring users to re-scan QR codes.

nodes.name: sendMessage
nodes.summary: Sends a WhatsApp text message to a phone number via an active user session, normalising the number to the Baileys JID format and throwing if the session is not connected.

nodes.name: AutoRefresher
nodes.summary: Default-exported client component that wires useAutoRefresh to periodically call router.refresh(). Renders null.

nodes.name: AdminPage
nodes.summary: Async server component that guards the admin route: redirects unauthenticated or non-admin users, then renders AdminClient.

nodes.name: normalizeApolloPhone
nodes.summary: Normalizes a raw phone string from Apollo by stripping non-digit characters.

nodes.name: releaseConnectSlot
nodes.summary: Releases a prospecting run connect slot, allowing the scheduler to queue the next connection.

nodes.name: shouldSkipSeed
nodes.summary: Returns true if seeding should be skipped based on existing contact count and force flag.

nodes.name: pollTask
nodes.summary: Polls the backend for a pending task (SEND, CHECK_REPLY, SEARCH, CONNECT). Returns null when idle.

nodes.name: reportResult
nodes.summary: Reports the result of a completed task back to the backend API.

nodes.name: openTabInAutomationWindow
nodes.summary: Opens a URL as a new tab in the automation window, returning the new tab ID.

nodes.name: getApiBase
nodes.summary: Retrieves the stored API base URL from extension storage, defaulting to the production URL.

tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: The README is the best starting point for understanding what this platform does and why it exists. It covers the end-to-end story: import LinkedIn connections as a CSV, auto-enrich contacts with email and phone via HubSpot and Apollo, then run targeted outreach through LinkedIn messages, WhatsApp, or Email using campaigns and multi-step drip sequences. Reading it first gives you the vocabulary and mental model needed to make sense of every subsequent file in the tour.

tour.title: Application Entry Point
tour.description: The root Next.js layout in `app/layout.tsx` is the shell that wraps every page in the application. It sets global document attributes (RTL support, fonts), mounts the session provider, and establishes the outermost HTML structure. Starting here grounds you in the App Router convention used throughout: every feature lives under `app/`, with server components doing data-fetching and client components handling interactivity.
tour.languageLesson: Next.js App Router uses a file-system layout hierarchy — every `layout.tsx` in a folder wraps all routes beneath it. The root layout is rendered once and persists across navigations, making it the right place for global providers and fonts.

tour.title: Authentication & Multi-Tenancy
tour.description: Two files work together to secure every request in the platform. `lib/auth.ts` configures NextAuth with a Prisma adapter, wires session callbacks, and supports admin impersonation — the mechanism that lets an admin act as any tenant user. `lib/tenancy/with-tenant.ts` is the higher-order wrapper that every API route must use: it authenticates the request, resolves the effective user (respecting impersonation), and exposes a `ctx` object with the tenant-scoped Prisma client. This is the most depended-upon file in the codebase (fan-in: 54), so understanding it is essential before reading any route handler.
tour.languageLesson: Higher-order functions that wrap async route handlers are a common TypeScript pattern for cross-cutting concerns. The `withTenant` wrapper uses generics to preserve the inner handler's type signature while injecting a typed `ctx` argument, avoiding any loss of type safety at the call site.

tour.title: Data Model & Prisma Client
tour.description: The Prisma schema is the canonical definition of every entity in the system — 25+ models covering `Organization`, `User`, `Contact`, `Company`, `Sequence`, `SequenceStep`, `SequenceEnrollment`, `SentMessage`, `ProspectingRun`, `ImportJob`, and more. `lib/prisma.ts` provides the singleton Prisma client instance used throughout the server-side code, reusing a global reference in development to avoid connection exhaustion during hot reload. `lib/generated/prisma/client.ts` is the auto-generated Prisma output that exposes the fully-typed client class — you never edit it, but it is imported everywhere and its fan-in of 110 makes it the single most referenced file in the project.
tour.languageLesson: Prisma generates a fully-typed client from the schema, meaning TypeScript catches schema mismatches at compile time. The schema also drives database migrations — `prisma migrate dev` produces SQL diffs automatically from model changes.

tour.title: Contacts UI: Server + Client Split
tour.description: The contacts list demonstrates the App Router server/client split at its most developed. `app/(dashboard)/contacts/page.tsx` is a server component: it reads the session, builds tenant-scoped Prisma where-clauses from URL search params, and fetches the first page of contacts before rendering. `contacts-client.tsx` receives that data as props and takes over with client-side state: filters, pagination, row selection, bulk enrichment triggers, and auto-refresh. The `contact-drawer.tsx` component renders the detailed side-panel for a single contact, composing multiple sections (info, enrichment status, messages history, list membership) into one rich view.
tour.languageLesson: React Server Components (RSC) allow data fetching at the component level without client-side waterfalls. The server component pre-fetches the first page of data, which is serialized and streamed to the client — React 19's `use` hook and Suspense then handle subsequent async boundaries.

tour.title: Contacts API Routes
tour.description: The contacts API routes in `app/api/contacts/` show exactly how `withTenant` is applied in practice. `route.ts` handles the collection endpoint: `GET` with rich filtering and pagination, and `POST` to create contacts with automatic HubSpot sync. `[id]/route.ts` handles per-contact `GET` and `PATCH`, including merging manually-edited fields. Every query in these handlers filters by `ctx.effectiveUserId`, enforcing the tenancy rule that ensures no tenant can ever see another's data.

tour.title: CSV Import Pipeline
tour.description: The import flow is the platform's first contact with raw LinkedIn data. `app/api/import/csv/route.ts` accepts an uploaded connections CSV from the browser and immediately hands off to an Inngest `import.process` event — the API response is instant and the heavy lifting happens asynchronously in the background. `inngest/functions/import-process.ts` does the real work: it parses the CSV, diffs new rows against existing contacts, classifies industry and seniority, and upserts records into the database. This pattern — thin API route, background Inngest function — repeats throughout the platform for any operation that might take more than a few seconds.
tour.languageLesson: Offloading work to a background queue via a short-lived API route is a key serverless pattern. It avoids HTTP timeout limits (typically 10-30s on hosting platforms) and gives the background job its own retry, timeout, and observability budget.

tour.title: Contact Enrichment
tour.description: After import, contacts are bare-bones — just name and LinkedIn URL. The enrichment pipeline fills in email, phone, and company data. `lib/hubspot/client.ts` and `lib/apollo/client.ts` are the two external service clients: HubSpot looks up contacts by LinkedIn URL, email, or name; Apollo performs person enrichment with phone-number selection and mobile-number reveal. `inngest/functions/enrich-contact.ts` orchestrates the multi-step enrichment for a single contact — calling HubSpot first, then Apollo if needed, and writing results back through the budgeted spend tracker. This is the fan-in leader among service clients (28 inbound references), reflecting how central enrichment is to the platform's value.

tour.title: Background Job Infrastructure (Inngest)
tour.description: Inngest is the backbone for all asynchronous work in the platform. `inngest/client.ts` exports the singleton Inngest client used everywhere to fire events. `app/api/inngest/route.ts` is the single registration endpoint that Inngest's server polls — it lists every background function (enrichment, campaigns, sequences, prospecting, imports, job-change checks) so they can receive events. Understanding these two files tells you the contract between the API layer and every background function: fire an event via `inngest.send()`, and the registered function runs in the background with automatic retries and observability.
tour.languageLesson: Inngest uses a push-based event model: your API fires an event, and Inngest delivers it to all registered handlers. Functions can `step.run()` to checkpoint progress — if the function fails mid-way, Inngest replays from the last successful step rather than restarting from scratch.

tour.title: Campaign & Sequence Builder
tour.description: The `campaign-builder.tsx` component is the primary authoring UI for outreach sequences. It lets users define a multi-step drip sequence — mixing LinkedIn messages, WhatsApp messages, and emails — with configurable delays between steps and a chosen contact list as the audience. On the backend, `inngest/functions/sequence-start.ts` is triggered when a sequence is activated: it parses the step definitions and schedules all enrollment execution records with their spaced send times. The `sequence-tick.ts` cron function then fires periodically to find due executions and dispatch `sequence.send-execution` events, which `sequence-send-execution.ts` processes one at a time.

tour.title: Message Dispatch Engine
tour.description: The actual sending logic lives in `lib/sequences/execute-send.ts`, which is called by the `sequence-send-execution` function. It is the platform's most complex service function (fan-out: 16): it gates on whether prior steps in the sequence have completed, enforces daily send quotas and send-window time constraints, renders the message template with contact variable substitution, and dispatches via Gmail API or WhatsApp client depending on the step type. LinkedIn sends are handled differently — they are queued as extension tasks for the Chrome extension to execute. This file is the convergence point for all three outreach channels.

tour.title: Prospecting Automation
tour.description: Prospecting is the platform's outbound discovery feature — it drives LinkedIn search, scrapes matching profiles, and sends connection requests automatically. `inngest/functions/prospecting-start.ts` initializes a prospecting run by building a LinkedIn search URL and queuing the first connect slot. `lib/prospecting/connect-scheduler.ts` orchestrates the pacing: it enforces daily and hourly quotas and queues the next connection request as an extension task. `inngest/functions/prospecting-tick.ts` is the cron driver (every 5 minutes) that advances active runs, releasing slots as earlier connections are processed.

tour.title: Chrome Extension: LinkedIn Automation
tour.description: The Chrome extension is the only component that can actually interact with LinkedIn's UI, since LinkedIn does not expose a public API for sending messages or connection requests. `extension/src/background.ts` is the extension's service worker: it polls the backend for pending automation tasks and drives LinkedIn — sending messages, accepting connection requests, and scraping search results. `extension/src/lib/cdp.ts` is the low-level Chrome Debugger Protocol helper that makes it all possible: it simulates human-like click, type, and keypress events, manages tab lifecycle, and provides high-level LinkedIn DOM interaction helpers used by the task-execution code.
tour.languageLesson: Chrome Manifest V3 extensions use a service worker instead of a persistent background page — the service worker can be terminated and restarted by the browser at any time, so state must be persisted to `chrome.storage` rather than in-memory variables.

tour.title: WhatsApp Sidecar Service
tour.description: WhatsApp cannot be automated via a browser extension, so the platform runs a dedicated Express microservice using the Baileys library (which reverse-engineers the WhatsApp Web protocol). `whatsapp-service/src/index.ts` exposes REST and SSE endpoints for session management: QR code pairing, connect/disconnect, and outbound message sending. `whatsapp-service/src/session-manager.ts` manages the per-user session lifecycle — handling QR auth-state streaming, automatic reconnection, and cleanup. The main Next.js app communicates with this sidecar via `lib/whatsapp/client.ts`, keeping the channel-specific complexity fully isolated.
tour.languageLesson: Server-Sent Events (SSE) are a lightweight alternative to WebSockets for server-to-client streaming — the server holds a persistent HTTP connection and pushes newline-delimited `data:` lines. SSE is ideal for progress streams like WhatsApp QR pairing status where the client only needs to receive, not send.

tour.title: Infrastructure & Deployment
tour.description: The `Dockerfile` uses a three-stage build: a `deps` stage installs packages and generates the Prisma client, a `builder` stage compiles the Next.js app, and a minimal `runner` stage copies only the production artifacts — keeping the final image small and secure. `docker-compose.yml` orchestrates the full stack locally and in production: PostgreSQL 16, the WhatsApp sidecar, and the Next.js app, all wired together with environment variables and a shared network. The GitHub Actions `deploy.yml` workflow closes the loop: on every push to `main`, it fires a Coolify webhook that pulls the latest image and rolls out a zero-downtime deployment.
tour.languageLesson: Multi-stage Docker builds are the standard for production Node.js images. Separating the build stage (which needs compilers, dev deps, and Prisma CLI) from the runtime stage (which only needs the compiled output and production deps) typically reduces final image size by 60-80%.
